claim: Dopamine neurons respond to errors in predicting value-neutral sensory information.
source: Dopamine neurons respond to errors in predicting value-neutral sensory information.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Dopamine transients support sensory-based associative learning.
source: These data, combined with causal evidence that dopamine transients support sensory-based associative learning, suggest that the dopamine system signals a multidimensional prediction error.
evidence: This claim is supported by causal evidence mentioned in the text and is presented as established knowledge.

claim: The dopamine system signals a multidimensional prediction error.
source: These data, combined with causal evidence that dopamine transients support sensory-based associative learning, suggest that the dopamine system signals a multidimensional prediction error.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combination of data on sensory prediction errors and causal evidence of dopamine's role in learning.

claim: The complexity of multidimensional prediction errors is not evident in the activity of individual neurons or population averages.
source: Yet such complexity is not evident in the activity of individual neurons or population averages.
evidence: This claim is presented as an observation from prior research and sets up the research question.

claim: The pattern of firing across a small group of dopamine neurons recorded in rats signals the identity of a mis-predicted sensory event.
source: Consistent with this, here we show that the pattern of firing across a small group of dopamine neurons recorded in rats signals the identity of a mis-predicted sensory event.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from rat recordings.

claim: Information about mis-predicted sensory events is reflected in the BOLD response elicited by sensory prediction errors in human midbrain.
source: Further, this same information is reflected in the BOLD response elicited by sensory prediction errors in human midbrain.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by fMRI data from human subjects.

claim: Ensembles of dopamine neurons provide highly specific teaching signals.
source: These data provide evidence that ensembles of dopamine neurons provide highly specific teaching signals, opening new possibilities for how this system might contribute to learning.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings showing content-specific information in ensemble activity.

claim: Midbrain dopamine neurons are widely proposed to signal value prediction errors.
source: Midbrain dopamine neurons are widely proposed to signal value prediction errors (Mirenowicz and Schultz, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Dopamine neurons respond to errors in predicting the features of rewarding events, even when their value remains unchanged.
source: However, the same neurons also respond to errors in predicting the features of rewarding events, even when their value remains unchanged (Howard and Kahnt, 2018; Takahashi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Sensory prediction errors would be useful for learning detailed information about the relationships between real-world events.
source: Such sensory prediction errors would be useful for learning detailed information about the relationships between real-world events (Gardner et al., 2018; Howard and Kahnt, 2018; Langdon et al., 2018; Takahashi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents a theoretical inference about the function of sensory prediction errors.

claim: Dopamine transients facilitate learning relationships between events independent of value when appropriately positioned to mimic endogenous errors.
source: Indeed, dopamine transients facilitate learning such relationships, independent of value, when they are appropriately positioned to mimic endogenous errors (Chang et al., 2017; Keiflin et al., 2019; Sharpe et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to causal experimental studies.

claim: Dopaminergic responses to sensory prediction errors do not encode the content of the mis-predicted event at the level of individual neurons or summed across populations.
source: Yet dopaminergic responses to sensory prediction errors do not seem to encode the content of the mis-predicted event, either at the level of individual neurons or summed across populations (Howard and Kahnt, 2018; Takahashi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research findings.

claim: Information about the content of learning might be contained in the pattern of firing across ensembles of dopamine neurons.
source: However, another possibility is that information about the content of the learning might be contained, at least partly, in the pattern of firing across ensembles of dopamine neurons.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors that is tested in the study.

claim: Information is represented in areas like cortex and hippocampus in a distributed fashion in the firing of groups of cells.
source: It is now widely accepted that information is represented in areas like cortex and hippocampus not by individual neurons, but rather in a distributed fashion in the firing of groups of cells (Gochin et al., 1994; Jennings et al., 2019; Jones et al., 2007; Rich and Wallis, 2016; Rigotti et al., 2013; Schoenbaum and Eichenbaum, 1995; Wikenheiser and Redish, 2015; Wilson and McNaughton, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: Rats were highly accurate in choosing the rewarded well during recording, with approximately 95% correct responses.
source: During recording, the rats were highly accurate, responding correctly on ~95% of the forced-choice trials, indicating that they had learned the meaning of the odor cues, independent of reward number or flavor (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the experiment shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Rats' accuracy in choosing the rewarded well was unaffected by the flavor or number of drops at a particular well.
source: Rats were highly accurate in choosing the rewarded well during recording (b), and accuracy was unaffected by the flavor or number of drops at a particular well, either for the group or for individual subjects (flavor: F1,193=1.3, p=0.26; number: F1,193=1.0, p=0.32; interactions with subject: F's <= 1.0, p's > 0.47).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Rats responded significantly faster when the 3-drop reward was at stake compared to the 1-drop reward.
source: The rats also exhibited an appreciation of the reward number, responding significantly faster when the 3-drop reward was at stake, an effect that was also independent of the reward flavor (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the experiment shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Rats' response latency was similar across the two flavors, even in the behavior of individual rats.
source: Indeed, choice latency was similar across the two flavors, even in the behavior of individual rats, suggesting that they valued the two flavors similarly in the task (Figure 1c, lines).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the experiment shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Rats had no significant preference between the two flavors of Kool-Aid in preference testing conducted after recording.
source: This is consistent with preference testing conducted separately after recording, which indicated that individually and as a group the rats had no significant preference between the two flavors of Kool-Aid (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from preference testing shown in Figure 1d.

claim: 30 putative dopaminergic neurons were identified using waveform characteristics and firing in response to reward.
source: Using waveform characteristics and firing in response to reward, as in previous papers (see Materials and methods), we identified 30 putative dopaminergic neurons recorded during these sessions (Figure 1e and f and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the methods used for neuron identification and the data shown in Figure 1e, f and Table 1.

claim: The firing of dopamine neurons exhibited classic reward prediction error correlates, decreasing in response to reward omission and increasing in response to unexpected reward.
source: As previously reported (Takahashi et al., 2017 in Supplemental Figure 2), the firing of these neurons exhibited classic reward prediction error correlates, decreasing in response to reward omission at the first transition and increasing in response to unexpected reward at the second transition, changes that were inversely correlated across neurons (Figure 2a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 2a-c and citation to prior work.

claim: Changes in firing rate in response to omission and delivery were inversely correlated across neurons.
source: changes that were inversely correlated across neurons (Figure 2a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Individual dopamine neurons signal bidirectional errors in the prediction of reward in different species, tasks, and labs.
source: This is as expected based on numerous prior reports that individual dopamine neurons signal bidirectional errors in the prediction of reward, in different species, tasks, and labs (Schultz, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and represents established knowledge.

claim: Dopamine neurons exhibited increased firing rates in response to transitions in the expected flavor of reward.
source: In addition, however, the same neurons also responded with elevated firing across transitions in which there was a change in reward flavor, combining both the third transition, presented previously (Takahashi et al., 2017 in Supplemental Figure 2), and the more selective fourth transition, included here.
evidence: This claim is supported by neural recording data from the current study and prior work.

claim: Changes in dopamine neuron firing occurred in response to flavor changes even though rats' behavior indicated no difference in the subjective value of the two flavors.
source: These changes in firing occurred even though the rats' behavior – both in the task and in separate preference testing (Figure 1b–d) – indicated no difference in the subjective value of the two flavors, even for individual subjects.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combination of neural data and behavioral data showing no flavor preference.

claim: The size of increases in dopamine neuron firing to flavor changes were positively correlated between the two flavor errors.
source: The dopamine neurons increased firing to changes in flavor, and the size of these increases were positively correlated between the two flavor errors (Figure 2d and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Individual dopamine neurons showed very little difference between initial firing rates in response to the two different flavor errors.
source: Further, individual neurons showed very little difference between initial firing rates in response to the two different flavor errors (Figure 2f).
evidence: This claim is supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The activity of individual dopamine neurons or their average signaled that something unexpected had happened, but did not distinguish details of that event.
source: Thus, the activity of these neurons, individually or on average, signaled that something unexpected had happened, but it did not distinguish details of that event (e.g. if grape was switched for tropical punch or vice versa).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the neural recording data showing similar responses to different flavor errors.

claim: The pattern of activity across the dopamine neuron ensemble contained information about flavor in both of the flavor-change trial blocks.
source: The results indicated that the pattern of activity across the ensemble did contain information about flavor in both of the flavor-change trial blocks (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis of neural ensemble data shown in Figure 3a and b.

claim: Accurate decoding of flavor was observed only for the drops where flavor had changed and only on trials early in the blocks.
source: Critically, however, accurate decoding of flavor was observed only for the drops where flavor had changed and then only on trials early in the blocks; accuracy was only seen in epochs immediately after the new drop was delivered and fell to chance later in the block, consistent with representation of the error in predicting the flavor – either the omission of the expected flavor or the delivery of the new flavor - and not representation of flavor itself.
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis of neural ensemble data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Flavor could be decoded accurately by dopamine ensembles only immediately after changes in flavor.
source: This effect was also evident when we collapsed data from the two blocks and compared decoding in epochs capturing firing to the drops where flavor changed versus control epochs capturing firing where flavors had not changed (c); flavor could be decoded accurately by dopamine ensembles only immediately after changes in flavor (patterns in confusion matrices were significantly different at p<10−4 by permutation test).
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 3c with statistical testing.

claim: Accurate decoding of flavor was only observed when the drop had changed flavor, and only in the first 10 trials of these blocks.
source: Accurate decoding was only observed when the drop had changed flavor, and then only in the first 10 trials of these blocks; decoding was best in the earliest trials immediately after the transition, fell to chance in the last 10 trials, and flavors from the early trials did not misclassify with the same flavors in the later trials (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 3c and d.

claim: Flavor could be decoded from neural activity in early trials as early as 175 ms after fluid delivery.
source: Separate analyses indicated that flavor could be decoded from neural activity in these early trials as early as 175 ms after fluid delivery (see Materials and methods for details of analysis).
evidence: This claim is supported by additional decoding analysis described in the methods.

claim: The decline in decoding accuracy across the block occurred without any gross changes in baseline firing rates.
source: The decline in decoding accuracy across the block occurred without any gross changes in baseline firing rates (Figure 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of firing rates shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The dopamine neuron ensemble was representing flavor when it had been mis-predicted, not the flavor itself.
source: Thus, the dopamine neuron ensemble was representing not the flavor itself, but flavor when it had been mis-predicted.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of decoding results showing flavor information only after unexpected changes.

claim: Sweet and savory food odors were matched in value, as reflected in pleasantness ratings acquired before the learning task.
source: The rewarding odors were matched in value, as reflected in both pleasantness ratings acquired before the learning task (Figure 4b) and choices made during the task (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from human subjects shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Sweet and savory food odors were matched in value, as reflected in choices made during the task.
source: The rewarding odors were matched in value, as reflected in both pleasantness ratings acquired before the learning task (Figure 4b) and choices made during the task (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from human subjects shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Odor switches evoked prediction error-like responses in the BOLD signal in the midbrain.
source: Previously it was reported that these switches evoked prediction error-like responses in the BOLD signal in the midbrain (Howard and Kahnt, 2018; Suarez et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: It was possible to decode the identity (SW or SV) of the unexpected odor from the midbrain activity at the time the error was experienced.
source: This analysis, which is conceptually similar to that applied to the single unit activity described above, found that it was possible to decode the identity (SW or SV) of the unexpected odor from the midbrain activity at the time the error was experienced (Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by MVPA analysis of fMRI data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Decoding of odor identity from midbrain activity was significantly above chance only on the trials in which the food odors were mis-predicted but at chance on subsequent trials when food odors were delivered as expected.
source: Importantly, decoding was significantly above chance only on the trials in which the food odors were mis-predicted but at chance on subsequent trials when food odors were delivered as expected (Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by MVPA analysis of fMRI data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Decoding was only above chance on the error trial, and the decoder was not biased towards prediction of a particular odor.
source: Follow-up examination of the decoder performance confirmed that decoding was only above chance on the error trial, and that the decoder was not biased towards prediction of a particular odor (Figure 4e), consistent with representation of the mis-predicted food odors and not the food odors themselves.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of decoder performance shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Putative dopaminergic sensory prediction error responses in the midbrain contain specific information about the features of the mis-predicted event itself in both rats and humans.
source: The results presented here show that, in both rats and humans, putative dopaminergic sensory prediction error responses in the midbrain contain specific information about the features of the mis-predicted event itself, appropriate for instructing or updating representations in downstream brain regions.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the experimental data from both rat and human studies.

claim: The midbrain dopamine system signals a multidimensional prediction error, able to reflect a failure to predict information about an unexpected event beyond and even orthogonal to value.
source: These results are consistent with the proposal that the midbrain dopamine system signals a multidimensional prediction error, able to reflect a failure to predict information about an unexpected event beyond and even orthogonal to value (Gardner et al., 2018; Howard and Kahnt, 2018; Langdon et al., 2018; Takahashi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the current results and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The multidimensional prediction error proposal can account for value errors as a special example of a more general function.
source: Importantly this proposal is not necessarily contrary to current canon; it can account for value errors as a special example of a more general function (Gardner et al., 2018), one readily apparent in the firing of individual neurons perhaps due to the priority given to such information when it is the goal of the experimental subject.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim inferred from the results and supported by citation.

claim: The multidimensional prediction error proposal explains why dopamine neurons are often phasically active in settings where value errors were not anticipated, such as when novel cues or information is first presented.
source: However, this proposal also explains in a relatively straightforward way why dopamine neurons are often phasically active in settings where value errors were not anticipated a priori, at least by the experimenters, such as when novel cues or even information is first presented (Bromberg-Martin and Hikosaka, 2009; Horvitz, 2000; Horvitz et al., 1997; Kakade and Dayan, 2002), or even in response to violations in beliefs or auditory expectations (Gläscher et al., 2010; Gold et al., 2019; Iglesias et al., 2013; Schwartenbeck et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim that explains prior observations, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The pattern of firing across a relatively small population of dopamine neurons can provide details regarding the mis-predicted event, endowing the dopamine system with the ability to serve as an instructive 'teaching' signal outside the dimension of value.
source: That the pattern of firing across a relatively small population of dopamine neurons can provide details regarding the mis-predicted event endows the dopamine system with the ability to serve as an instructive 'teaching' signal outside the dimension of value.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings showing content-specific information in ensemble activity.

claim: The information about mis-predicted events in dopamine neuron activity is only present when it is relevant to learning at the start of the blocks.
source: While the current data is only correlative, it is notable that the information is only there when it is relevant to learning at the start of the blocks, so it is appropriately positioned to be of use to drive learning in downstream structures.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the temporal pattern of decoding accuracy shown in the results.

claim: A causal role for the dopamine signal in learning is in line with recent demonstrations that dopamine transients are necessary and sufficient for learning that cannot be easily accounted for by classic reinforcement learning mechanisms.
source: And of course, a causal role for the signal shown here is in line with recent demonstrations that dopamine transients are necessary and sufficient for learning that cannot be easily accounted for by classic reinforcement learning mechanisms (Chang et al., 2017; Keiflin et al., 2019; Sharpe et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior causal studies.

claim: Artificial activation of VTA dopamine neurons induced the formation of an association between the conditioned stimulus and the sensory properties (flavor) of the reward.
source: Keiflin et al. (2019) is particularly relevant in this regard, since in this study, conditioned responding to a cue unblocked by artificial activation of VTA dopamine neurons at the time of an expected reward was shown to be sensitive to subsequent devaluation of that reward. Sensitivity to devaluation indicates that the artificial dopamine transients induced the formation of an association between the conditioned stimulus and the sensory properties (i.e. the flavor) of the reward, precisely the type of learning the signal here would be proposed to support (Gardner et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the results of a cited study and the current findings.

claim: There are approximately 40,000 dopamine neurons in the VTA of rats, and another 25,000 in SN.
source: There are approximately 40,000 dopamine neurons in the VTA of rats, and another 25,000 in SN (Nair-Roberts et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior anatomical work.

claim: In humans, the total number of dopamine neurons is about 300,000.
source: In humans, the total number is about 300,000 (Hirsch et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior anatomical work.

claim: The demonstration of distributed, multidimensional error signaling in dopamine neurons mirrors advances in the computational field, where such signaling is a key component of more advanced algorithms like distributed reinforcement learning and successor representation.
source: Finally it is worth noting that the demonstration here mirrors advances in the computational field, where distributed, multidimensional error signaling is a key component of more advanced algorithms, such as distributed reinforcement learning and successor representation (Dabney et al., 2017; Dayan, 1993).
evidence: This claim draws a parallel between the current findings and computational models, supported by citations.

claim: Distributed reinforcement learning has recently been suggested as an explanation for the heterogeneity of the responses of individual dopamine neurons to errors in predicting reward value.
source: Distributed reinforcement learning has recently been suggested as an explanation for the heterogeneity of the responses of individual dopamine neurons to errors in predicting reward value (Kurth-Nelson et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent computational work.

claim: An assembly of dopamine neurons can function to represent the content of errors, even outside the realm of value.
source: The current results extend this to show for the first time that an assembly of dopamine neurons can function to represent the content of errors, even outside the realm of value.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: The same information available in the pattern of activity is not readily apparent in the activity of individual neurons.
source: That the same information available in the pattern of activity is not readily apparent in the activity of individual neurons is in accord with ideas guiding behavioral neurophysiology in other areas (Yuste, 2015), and suggests it is time to consider the functions of the dopamine system across rather than within individual neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the results and supported by citation to work on ensemble coding.

claim: Changes in firing rate in response to omission (negative errors) and delivery (positive errors) were readily distinguishable (t29 = 4.0, p<10−3).
source: Changes in firing rate in response to omission (negative errors) and delivery (positive errors) were readily distinguishable (a; t29 = 4.0, p<10−3)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of neural data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Firing rates of dopamine neurons were markedly different after the transition in reward number (t29 = 5.2, p<10−4).
source: and firing rates were markedly different after the transition (c; t29 = 5.2, p<10−4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of neural data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Dopamine neurons exhibited increased firing rates in response to transitions in the expected flavor of reward (t29 = 2.1, p<0.05).
source: The same neurons exhibited increased firing rates in response to transitions in the expected flavor of reward (d); t29 = 2.1, p<0.05)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of neural data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The increases in dopamine neuron firing to the two flavors were indistinguishable (t29 = −1.95, ns).
source: but the increases to the two flavors were indistinguishable (t29 = −1.95, ns)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of neural data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Firing rates of dopamine neurons after the flavor transition did not distinguish the two flavor errors (t29 = 0.13, ns).
source: and firing rates after the transition also did not distinguish the two flavor errors (f; t29 = 0.13, ns).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of neural data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Sweet and savory food odors at high concentration did not differ significantly in pleasantness (t22 = 0.18, p=0.86).
source: Sweet and savory food odors were matched for pleasantness within each odor concentration (SW high vs. SV high: t22 = 0.18, p=0.86; SW low vs. SV low: t22 = 1.16, p=0.26).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of pleasantness ratings shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Sweet and savory food odors at low concentration did not differ significantly in pleasantness (t22 = 1.16, p=0.26).
source: Sweet and savory food odors were matched for pleasantness within each odor concentration (SW high vs. SV high: t22 = 0.18, p=0.86; SW low vs. SV low: t22 = 1.16, p=0.26).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of pleasantness ratings shown in Figure 4b.

claim: On free choice trials, the cue associated with the high-concentration sweet odor was chosen significantly above chance (t22 = 4.03, p=2.83×10–4).
source: On free choice trials, the cue associated with the high-concentration odor was chosen significantly above chance (50%) for both odor identities (SW: t22 = 4.03, p=2.83×10–4; SV: t22 = 4.20, p=1.83×10−4)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of choice data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: On free choice trials, the cue associated with the high-concentration savory odor was chosen significantly above chance (t22 = 4.20, p=1.83×10−4).
source: On free choice trials, the cue associated with the high-concentration odor was chosen significantly above chance (50%) for both odor identities (SW: t22 = 4.03, p=2.83×10–4; SV: t22 = 4.20, p=1.83×10−4)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of choice data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Choice proportions for high-concentration sweet and savory odors did not differ significantly from each other (t22 = 0.71, p=0.48).
source: and these choice proportions did not differ significantly from each other (t22 = 0.71, p=0.48).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of choice data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Decoding accuracy of SW vs. SV was significantly above chance on the error trial of flavor transitions (t22 = 3.22, p=0.004).
source: Decoding accuracy of SW vs. SV was significantly above chance on the error trial of flavor transitions (black line) (t22 = 3.22, p=0.004), but not for subsequent trials or the trial preceding error trials (p's > 0.12).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of decoding data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Decoding accuracy of SW vs. SV was not significantly above chance for subsequent trials or the trial preceding error trials in flavor transitions (p's > 0.12).
source: Decoding accuracy of SW vs. SV was significantly above chance on the error trial of flavor transitions (black line) (t22 = 3.22, p=0.004), but not for subsequent trials or the trial preceding error trials (p's > 0.12).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of decoding data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Decoding accuracy of SW vs. SV was at chance for the error trial on value transitions, as well as subsequent trials and the trial preceding the value transitions (p's > 0.15).
source: Decoding accuracy of SW vs. SV was at chance for the error trial on value transitions (gray line), as well as subsequent trials, and the trial preceding the value transitions (p's > 0.15).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of decoding data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Within the training and testing on the error trial of flavor transitions, accuracy was at 63.3% for SW predictions and 63.8% for SV predictions across all subjects and iterations.
source: Within the top left quadrant of the flavor transition matrix (i.e. training and testing the classifier on the error trial of flavor transitions), across all subjects and iterations, accuracy was at 63.3% for SW predictions and 63.8% for SV predictions.
evidence: This claim is supported by detailed analysis of decoder performance shown in Figure 4e.
